summary: This review examines social hierarchies across species, covering how status is defined, formed, and perceived in nonhuman primates and humans. It compares perceptual cues like physical size, testosterone and posture with socio-cultural cues like job titles and education, and distinguishes dominance from prestige. The authors argue status strongly shapes attention, memory, health and social behavior, that adolescents may be especially sensitive to status, and that more neuroscience research on status processing in adolescents is needed.
one_line: A review of the neural and psychological foundations of social status perception across species, with emphasis on status cues and adolescent development.
key_facts: The review was published in Social Neuroscience in 2015 (volume 10, issue 5, pages 527–550) by Jessica Koski, Hongling Xie, and Ingrid R. Olson.
The article's DOI is 10.1080/17470919.2015.1013223 and its PMCID is PMC5494206.
The abstract states that social groups across species rapidly self-organize into hierarchies where members vary in power, influence, skill, or dominance.
The review states that humans use perceptual cues such as physical strength, and socio-cultural status cues such as job titles and educational attainment, to judge status.
The abstract states that one's relative status has profound effects on attention, memory, social interactions, as well as health and wellness.

The review defines rank as objectively referring to where one falls within the hierarchy, while status can be measured through social opinion or reputation and is associated with admiration and respect.
The review distinguishes dominance, a behavior or trait leading to power inequalities, from prestige, where individuals gain influence by demonstrating competence, knowledge, or skills without force.
Dominance is divided into sociable and aggressive subscales (Kalma, Visser, & Peeters, 1993).

In a longitudinal study of captive male vervet monkeys, males with lower levels of serotonin and dopamine metabolites before immigration into adult breeding groups were more likely to achieve higher status (Fairbanks et al., 2004).
The review cites findings that taller U.S. Presidential candidates are more likely to receive popular votes and to be reelected (Stulp, Buunk, Verhulst, & Pollet, 2012).
The review notes that Dalmaso and colleagues (2011) found participants more readily followed the gaze of high-status individuals, shown through fictive curriculum vitae.
The review states that when participants decide to help someone, they favor a lawyer (high status career title) over a gas station attendant (low status title) (Goodman & Gareis, 1993).
The abstract states that developmental research suggests teenagers may be particularly sensitive to social status information, but research on status processing and brain areas is very limited.
The review states its aims include examining status cues across non-human primate species to address the evolutionary origins of social hierarchies.
